C005.subject: Remote work
C005.object: individual task output per hour for tasks requiring spontaneous collaboration
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work individual task output per hour for tasks requiring spontaneous collaboration]

[PATH:empirical] A/B testing within a large tech firm comparing output per hour for spontaneous collaboration tasks (e.g., pair programming, quick code reviews) under fully remote vs. in-office conditions, controlling for task type and experience. — Directly measures the hypothesized effect in a real-world setting, isolating the impact of remote work on task output for collaboration-intensive tasks.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on communication latency and knowledge-sharing efficiency in distributed teams, drawing from organizational behavior and computer-supported cooperative work (CSCW) literature. — Synthesizes prior findings on how remote work affects ad-hoc collaboration, providing a broader evidence base to confirm or refute the hypothesized output decrease.

[PATH:empirical] Controlled lab experiment simulating spontaneous collaboration tasks (e.g., debugging a novel problem with a partner) in remote vs. co-located settings, measuring task completion time and output quality. — Allows causal inference under controlled conditions, isolating communication friction as a mechanism for output loss, thereby testing the hypothesis's core claim.

qualifier.tension: While structured tasks may benefit from fewer interruptions, tasks that rely on ad-hoc knowledge sharing or quick feedback loops suffer output loss due to communication friction in remote settings.

C006.subject: Remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work individual task output per hour]

[PATH:empirical] Bloom, N., Han, R., & Liang, J. (2022). 'How working from home works out.' Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research. (Or similar large-scale field experiment tracking individual output per hour via keystroke/log data.) — Provides direct, controlled comparison of individual task output (e.g., coding lines, writing word counts) per hour between remote and on-site settings, with pre-2020 baseline and post-2020 data, directly testing the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of remote work productivity studies (e.g., from meta-analyses in journals like Journal of Applied Psychology or Organization Science) focusing on individual-level output metrics (e.g., tasks completed per hour, error rates). — Aggregates multiple empirical studies to assess overall effect size and moderators (e.g., task complexity, self-discipline), reducing noise from single studies and clarifying whether the hypothesized decrease holds across contexts.

[PATH:empirical] Controlled experiment using a within-subject design with knowledge workers (e.g., programmers, writers) randomly assigned to remote vs. on-site days, with objective hourly output tracked via digital work logs and controlled for task difficulty. — Directly isolates the causal effect of remote work on per-hour output while controlling for confounds like self-selection or task variation, providing high internal validity to confirm or refute the hypothesis.

C007.subject: Remote work
C007.object: team collaboration efficiency more severely for newly formed teams than for established teams
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work team collaboration efficiency more severely for newly formed teams than for established teams]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field experiment comparing newly formed vs. established remote teams on a complex coordination task, measuring task completion time and communication frequency over the first 6 months. — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing the collaboration efficiency trajectories of new and established teams under remote work conditions, isolating the effect of pre-existing relational context.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on virtual team performance, focusing on moderators such as team tenure and prior co-location history. — Synthesizes available evidence to assess whether the purported differential impact is consistently observed across contexts, providing statistical power to confirm or refute the claim.

[PATH:theoretical] Agent-based simulation modeling the effects of communication modality (synchronous vs. asynchronous) on the development of shared mental models in new vs. established teams. — Tests the underlying causal mechanism: if asynchronous communication disproportionately delays mental model formation in new teams, the hypothesis is supported; if not, it is refuted.

qualifier.tension: New teams lack pre-existing relational context and shared mental models, making asynchronous communication even more costly for joint problem-solving compared to teams with prior co-located history.

C008.subject: Remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work team collaboration efficiency]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field experiment comparing matched teams working remotely vs. in-office on real-time coordination tasks (e.g., software development sprints, crisis response simulations) — Direct causal evidence from controlled assignment and repeated measures can isolate the effect of remote work on collaboration efficiency, addressing the disputed status and the temporal scope (2021–2024).

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of survey and productivity data from knowledge-economy firms (e.g., GitLab, Microsoft, Upwork) on team communication frequency, project completion times, and perceived coordination quality — Synthesizing existing large-scale datasets across sectors and geographies can reveal whether the hypothesized enhancement holds consistently or is moderated by task type, team size, or technology infrastructure.

[PATH:theoretical] Agent-based simulation modeling team coordination under varying remote work conditions (e.g., async communication delays, digital tool use, time zone dispersion) — Computational modeling can test mechanisms (e.g., information loss, coordination overhead) that might explain or refute the net efficiency gain, especially for real-time tasks, and generate predictions for empirical testing.
